questions.stem: A trolley moves to the right along a smooth horizontal track, and its speed increases steadily from rest. Which statement about the net horizontal force acting on the trolley is necessarily true?

options.A: The net horizontal force is strictly non-zero and points to the right.
options.B: The net horizontal force is zero because the speed increase is steady.
options.C: The net horizontal force must exceed the forward momentum of the trolley.
options.D: The net horizontal force points to the left to balance the forward inertia.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-01 to APPLY demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Speeding up rightward implies acceleration is directed rightward; by Newton II, $\Sigma F_{\text{net}} = m a_x > 0$.

B.diagnostic: Confuses constant speed with steadily changing speed; steady speed increase means non-zero constant acceleration.

C.diagnostic: Confuses force with momentum; force has dimensions of [M L T^-2] while momentum is [M L T^-1].

D.diagnostic: Invents a fictitious opposing force of inertia in an inertial frame.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: The trolley is moving right and speeding up. What does that tell you about the direction of its acceleration?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Its acceleration points to the right, the same direction as the velocity while the speed increases.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: For one chosen trolley, what representation connects that acceleration to the forces acting on it?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Draw the trolley FBD and form the horizontal vector sum $\Sigma F_x$.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What law would you write first after determining the acceleration direction?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Write $\Sigma F_x = m a_x$. Use the acceleration direction from H1 only after you have written the law.

reasoning_ladder.understand: The velocity magnitude is increasing to the right, so acceleration is rightward.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Use one trolley FBD and the horizontal axis.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton II requires $\Sigma F_x = m a_x$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Since $a_x > 0$, $\Sigma F_x > 0$: the net horizontal force is rightward.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: A rightward net force is required; individual forces need not all point right.

model_proof.final_expression: The net horizontal force is strictly non-zero and points to the right.
model_proof.final_answer_value: The net horizontal force is strictly non-zero and points to the right.

independent_check.quick_check: If the net force were zero, the velocity could not be changing.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: A leftward net force would make a right-moving trolley slow down, not speed up.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not infer force direction from velocity alone; use the change of velocity.

questions.stem: A student standing on the ground pushes horizontally against a rigid vertical wall with a force of $120\text{ N}$. What force does the wall exert on the student?

figure.caption: Figure 2: Newton III reciprocal interaction pair between student and wall.

options.A: Exactly $120\text{ N}$ directed horizontally away from the wall (opposite the push).
options.B: Zero, because the wall is fixed and does not accelerate or move.
options.C: Less than $120\text{ N}$, because the wall absorbs energy elastically.
options.D: More than $120\text{ N}$, because the wall is much more massive than the student.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-08 to EXPLAIN demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Newton III mandates that the mutual interaction between student and wall consists of equal and opposite forces: F_(student by wall) = -F_(wall by student) = 120 N away from wall.

B.diagnostic: Confuses absence of acceleration of the wall with absence of contact reaction force.

C.diagnostic: Claims contact force depends on material elasticity rather than universal 3rd law reciprocity.

D.diagnostic: Believes more massive or rigid bodies exert greater interaction forces than lighter ones.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: The student and wall are one interaction pair. What does Newton III say about the two interaction forces?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: They are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different bodies.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How would you label the pair so body ownership cannot be confused?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Use 'force on wall by student' and 'force on student by wall'.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If the student-on-wall force is +120 N, what relation would you write first for the wall-on-student force?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: F_(student by wall) = -F_(wall by student).

reasoning_ladder.understand: This is one contact interaction between two bodies: student and wall.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Represent the pair on two different bodies with explicit vectors.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton III: F(on student by wall) = -F(on wall by student).
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Magnitude is therefore 120 N, opposite the push direction.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The wall exerts 120 N horizontally on the student away from the wall.

model_proof.final_expression: Exactly $120\text{ N}$ directed horizontally away from the wall (opposite the push).
model_proof.final_answer_value: Exactly $120\text{ N}$ directed horizontally away from the wall (opposite the push).

independent_check.quick_check: The two forces are equal even if the wall barely accelerates.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: The student acceleration depends on the net force on the student, not on 'cancelling' this pair.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not put both third-law forces on the same FBD.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A cricket ball of mass $m = 0.40\text{ kg}$ traveling horizontally at $v_i = 15\text{ m/s}$ is caught and brought to rest. Compare the magnitude of the average force exerted on the fielder's hands if the ball is stopped in $\Delta t_1 = 0.10\text{ s}$ versus cushioned over $\Delta t_2 = 0.30\text{ s}$.

options.A: 60 N in the 0.10 s catch versus 20 N in the 0.30 s catch (one-third the force).
options.B: 6.0 N in both catches because the momentum change is identical.
options.C: 180 N in the 0.10 s catch versus 60 N in the 0.30 s catch.
options.D: 20 N in the 0.10 s catch versus 60 N in the 0.30 s catch.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-07 to APPLY demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

B.diagnostic: Confuses impulse $\Delta p$ = 6 N*s with average force $F_{\text{avg}}$ in Newtons.

C.diagnostic: Multiplied by velocity twice or made an arithmetic scaling error.

D.diagnostic: Inverted the time dependency, assuming longer impact duration increases contact force.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: The initial and final momenta are the same in both catches. What quantity changes between the two cases?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Only the stopping time changes; the momentum change is the same.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which state representation makes the sign and size of the momentum change explicit?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Write $p_i$ = m v_i, $p_f$ = 0, then $\Delta p$ = $p_f$ - $p_i$ for each case.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What force relation would you write first once $\Delta p$ is known?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $F_{\text{avg}}$ = $\Delta p$ / $\Delta t$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Same $\Delta p$ in both catches; only $\Delta t$ differs.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Take motion as positive: $p_i$ = 0.40(15) = 6 kg m/s and $p_f$ = 0.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Use $F_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$ with $\Delta p = -6\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Tripling stopping time reduces average force magnitude to one-third.

model_proof.final_expression: 60 N in the 0.10 s catch versus 20 N in the 0.30 s catch (one-third the force).
model_proof.final_answer_value: 60 N in the 0.10 s catch versus 20 N in the 0.30 s catch (one-third the force).

independent_check.quick_check: 60 * 0.10 = 20 * 0.30 = 6 N*s, the same impulse magnitude.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: A longer stopping time with the same impulse must lower average force.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not compare force using speed alone; compare $\Delta p$ and $\Delta t$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A passenger standing upright in an aisle of a city bus lurches forward when the driver brakes suddenly. Which statement explains this phenomenon correctly without inventing a fictitious forward force of inertia?

options.A: The passenger's body continues forward with its pre-braking velocity because no horizontal force acts on the upper torso until muscles or handrails intervene.
options.B: A forward 'force of inertia' is created by the braking system that pushes the passenger forward.
options.C: The bus exerts a forward reaction force on the passenger's feet to keep them moving.
options.D: Gravitational attraction shifts forward toward the front of the decelerating bus.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-01 to EXPLAIN demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: By Newton I, an object in motion continues with constant velocity in an inertial frame unless acted upon by a net external force; braking decelerates the bus and feet, while the upper body tends to retain pre-braking forward velocity.

B.diagnostic: Invents a fictitious forward force of inertia in an inertial frame.

C.diagnostic: Friction between bus floor and passenger feet acts backward to decelerate feet, not forward.

D.diagnostic: Gravity acts downward toward Earth's center and does not rotate forward during vehicle deceleration.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Immediately before braking, what horizontal velocity does the passenger's upper body already have?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The forward velocity of the bus relative to the road.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: When the bus decelerates, what horizontal contact force acts on the passenger's shoes from the floor?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Backward static friction decelerating the feet.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What horizontal force acts on the upper body before it tilts or grips a handrail?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Essentially zero; by Newton I, it tends to continue forward at constant velocity.

reasoning_ladder.understand: The passenger initially shares the bus forward velocity.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Represent the bus as slowing beneath the passenger; avoid a fictitious forward force in an inertial-frame FBD.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton I explains persistence of velocity until external forces change it.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Feet are decelerated by backward floor contact; the upper body continues forward briefly, producing the lurch.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The forward lurch is an inertia effect, not evidence of a new forward force.

model_proof.final_expression: The passenger's body continues forward with its pre-braking velocity because no horizontal force acts on the upper torso until muscles or handrails intervene.
model_proof.final_answer_value: The passenger's body continues forward with its pre-braking velocity because no horizontal force acts on the upper torso until muscles or handrails intervene.

independent_check.quick_check: If the bus braked gently over a longer time, the lurch would be smaller.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: The actual contact force during braking is backward on the passenger, not forward.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not invent a forward force of inertia in an inertial frame.

limiting_cases.expected: Feet also glide forward at constant pre-braking velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Inside a passenger train moving along a straight horizontal track with constant forward acceleration $a_0$, a seated passenger tosses a coin vertically upward. Relative to the passenger, where does the coin land?

options.A: Strictly behind the passenger's hand.
options.B: Exactly back into the passenger's hand.
options.C: In front of the passenger's hand.
options.D: To the right or left of the hand depending on the coin's spin.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-01 to MODEL demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Once airborne, gravity is the only force; the coin maintains its initial horizontal velocity $v_0$. Meanwhile, the train accelerates, covering a greater horizontal distance during the flight time $\Delta t$, so the floor and passenger advance ahead of the coin.

B.diagnostic: True only if the train moves at constant velocity (a = 0) in an inertial frame.

C.diagnostic: Would occur only if the train were decelerating (braking), not accelerating forward.

D.diagnostic: Lateral spin does not generate aerodynamic Magnus deflection in typical vertical coin tosses.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: While the coin is airborne, does it automatically share the train's continuing forward acceleration?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No; in flight, no horizontal force acts on the coin, so its horizontal velocity remains constant.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: During the flight time $\Delta t$, which covers a greater horizontal distance: the coin or the accelerating train?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The train, because its horizontal speed steadily increases while the coin's horizontal speed is fixed.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What coordinate difference x_train - x_coin develops over time $\Delta t$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\Delta x$ = 1/2 $a_0$ ($\Delta t$)^2 > 0 (train advances ahead of the coin).

reasoning_ladder.understand: The coin is launched vertically with horizontal velocity $v_0$ equal to the train's instantaneous velocity at launch.
reasoning_ladder.represent: In the ground frame, coin executes projectile motion with $v_x$ = $v_0$ = const, while train position is x_train = $v_0$ t + 1/2 $a_0$ t^2.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton I governs horizontal motion of coin ($\Sigma F_x = 0 \implies a_x = 0$).
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Relative horizontal position: x_coin,rel = x_coin - x_train = -1/2 $a_0$ t^2 < 0.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Because $\Delta x$ < 0, the coin lands behind the passenger.

model_proof.final_expression: Strictly behind the passenger's hand.
model_proof.final_answer_value: Strictly behind the passenger's hand.

independent_check.quick_check: If train acceleration $a_0$ = 0, the coin returns exactly to the hand.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: In the accelerating frame of the train, an apparent backward pseudo force F_pseudo = -m $a_0$ deflects the coin backward.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not assume airborne objects maintain the acceleration of their launch vehicle.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A hockey puck slides across a perfectly smooth, ideal frictionless horizontal ice rink with constant velocity $\vec{v} = 4.0\text{ m/s}\hat{i}$. What horizontal force is required to keep the puck moving at this constant velocity?

options.A: Exactly 0 N.
options.B: A forward force proportional to the puck's mass: F = m v.
options.C: A forward force equal to the puck's weight: F = mg.
options.D: A force equal to half the puck's kinetic energy: F = 1/2 m v^2.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-01 to RETRIEVE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: By Newton's First Law, an object in motion continues with constant velocity in an inertial frame when net force is zero; no sustaining force is needed.

B.diagnostic: Classical Aristotelian fallacy: believing force is needed to sustain constant motion.

C.diagnostic: Weight mg acts vertically downward, balanced by normal force N; no horizontal component exists.

D.diagnostic: Confuses energy in Joules with force in Newtons.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: The velocity of the puck is constant. What does Newton I say about constant velocity?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Constant velocity means acceleration is zero, which means net force is zero.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What vertical forces act on the puck, and do they balance?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Gravity downward and normal upward balance completely: N = mg.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What horizontal force is required to keep an object moving at constant velocity on a frictionless surface?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Zero Newtons.

reasoning_ladder.understand: The puck moves at constant velocity on a frictionless horizontal plane.
reasoning_ladder.represent: One-body FBD has downward mg and upward normal N. No horizontal interaction exists.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton I: $\Sigma F = 0$ when velocity is constant in an inertial frame.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Motion itself does not require a sustaining force; force is required only to change velocity.

model_proof.final_expression: Exactly 0 N.
model_proof.final_answer_value: Exactly 0 N.

independent_check.quick_check: If a forward force acted without friction, the puck would speed up, violating constant velocity.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: By work-energy theorem, W_net = Delta K = 0; since displacement > 0, $F_{\text{net}}$ must be 0.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not assume that moving objects automatically require a forward driving force.

limiting_cases.expected: F_applied = mu mg to maintain constant velocity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A chemical rocket drifts at constant velocity in deep interstellar space far from any celestial gravitational fields. When its engine fires, it ejects hot exhaust gases backward at high speed. Explain why the rocket accelerates forward.

options.A: Backward momentum of ejected exhaust gases must be balanced by forward momentum of the rocket, conserving total system momentum (Delta P_total = 0).
options.B: The ejected exhaust pushes backward against the surrounding vacuum of space, which pushes back on the rocket.
options.C: The rocket loses mass, which automatically increases its speed to keep kinetic energy constant.
options.D: Thermal expansion of hot gas inside the combustion chamber creates an electrostatic repulsive field.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-10 to MODEL demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Rocket + exhaust form an isolated system. Backward exhaust momentum $\Delta p_{\text{exhaust}}$ < 0 requires equal forward rocket momentum $\Delta p_{\text{rocket}}$ > 0.

B.diagnostic: Misconception that rockets require external atmosphere to push against; vacuum propulsion works by internal momentum exchange.

C.diagnostic: Kinetic energy is not conserved in chemical propulsion; chemical potential energy is converted to kinetic energy.

D.diagnostic: Rocket thrust is dynamic fluid momentum transfer, not electrostatic repulsion.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Which two parts exchange momentum during the short ejection event?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Rocket and exhaust.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the net external impulse acting on the rocket+exhaust system in deep space?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Zero, because there are no external gravitational or contact forces.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If the exhaust acquires backward momentum -$\Delta p$, what must the rocket acquire to keep total momentum constant?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: +$\Delta p$ (forward momentum).

reasoning_ladder.understand: The rocket and its fuel form an isolated multi-body system in deep space.
reasoning_ladder.represent: System boundary encloses rocket body and ejected exhaust gas.
reasoning_ladder.connect: System momentum conservation: $\Delta P_{\text{system}} = 0 \implies \Delta p_{\text{rocket}} + \Delta p_{\text{exhaust}} = 0$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: The rocket accelerates forward as a direct consequence of ejecting mass backward.

model_proof.final_expression: Backward momentum of ejected exhaust gases must be balanced by forward momentum of the rocket, conserving total system momentum (Delta P_total = 0).
model_proof.final_answer_value: Backward momentum of ejected exhaust gases must be balanced by forward momentum of the rocket, conserving total system momentum (Delta P_total = 0).

independent_check.quick_check: Forward rocket momentum balances backward exhaust momentum in the simplified system.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: By Newton III, nozzle walls exert a backward force on the gas; the expanding gas exerts an equal forward thrust on the nozzle.
independent_check.watch_out: Rockets do not need an atmosphere to push against; they push against their own expelled propellant.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A road tanker carrying water is filled to three-quarters of its capacity and travels along a straight level road. When the driver applies the brakes suddenly, in which direction does the water surge inside the tank?

options.A: The water surges forward toward the front of the tanker.
options.B: The water remains completely level because liquids cannot exhibit inertia.
options.C: The water surges backward toward the rear of the tanker.
options.D: The water compresses uniformly at the bottom of the tank without shifting forward or backward.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-01 to JUSTIFY demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: By Newton's First Law, the water possesses inertia of motion and continues with its pre-braking forward velocity relative to the road, surging forward against the decelerating tanker walls.

B.diagnostic: Fluids possess mass and therefore possess inertia identical to solids.

C.diagnostic: Water surges backward during forward acceleration, not during braking.

D.diagnostic: Water is essentially incompressible and exhibits free-surface sloshing.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Before braking, what velocity does the water already have relative to the road?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Approximately the tanker's forward velocity.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: When the tanker brakes, the tank walls decelerate. What horizontal force immediately decelerates the bulk water?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Only pressure forces once the water collides with the front bulkhead.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: By Newton's First Law, what does the water tend to do while the tanker slows down beneath it?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: It tends to maintain its forward speed, piling up toward the front of the tank.

reasoning_ladder.understand: The water initially shares the tanker's forward velocity.
reasoning_ladder.represent: In ground frame, the tanker decelerates (a_tank < 0) while bulk fluid continues at speed $v_0$.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton I: mass tends to persist in uniform motion until external forces act.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: Relative displacement Delta x_water = x_water - x_tank > 0.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Water surges forward toward the front bulkhead until pressure gradients balance deceleration.

model_proof.final_expression: The water surges forward toward the front of the tanker.
model_proof.final_answer_value: The water surges forward toward the front of the tanker.

independent_check.quick_check: Water surges toward the front during deceleration, exactly like a standing bus passenger.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: In the tanker's decelerating frame, a forward pseudo force F_pseudo = -m a_tank tilts the effective gravity forward.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not assume liquids behave differently from solids regarding Newton's First Law.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Three solid blocks $A$, $B$, and $C$ of identical exterior shape and dimensions have masses $m_A = 1.0\text{ kg}$, $m_B = 3.0\text{ kg}$, and $m_C = 5.0\text{ kg}$ respectively. Rank the blocks in order of increasing translational inertia.

options.A: A < B < C (1 kg < 3 kg < 5 kg).
options.B: C < B < A (5 kg < 3 kg < 1 kg).
options.C: A = B = C because all three blocks have identical volume and geometry.
options.D: Inertia depends only on velocity, so they cannot be ranked without knowing their speeds.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-04 to RETRIEVE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: In classical mechanics, mass is the quantitative measure of translational inertia; larger mass exhibits greater resistance to change in velocity.

B.diagnostic: Inverted the relationship between mass and inertia.

C.diagnostic: Confuses geometric volume with inertial mass.

D.diagnostic: Confuses momentum (mv) with inertia (m).

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What property measures resistance to a change in velocity in translational motion?

If the two masses are rigidly tied together and the same force $F = 5.0\text{ N}$ acts on the composite system, what acceleration is produced?

options.A: a_combined = 6.0 m/s^2.
options.B: a_combined = 16.0 m/s^2 (the arithmetic average).
options.C: a_combined = 32.0 m/s^2 (the sum of accelerations).
options.D: a_combined = 4.0 m/s^2.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-04 to SYNTHESIZE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

B.diagnostic: Arithmetic mean fallacy: averaged the accelerations (8+24)/2 = 16 m/s^2 instead of mass harmonic mean.

C.diagnostic: Added the accelerations together: 8 + 24 = 32 m/s^2; adding mass reduces acceleration, never increases it.

D.diagnostic: Arithmetic calculation error in fraction addition.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Force F = 5 N accelerates m1 at 8 m/s^2 and m2 at 24 m/s^2; find acceleration of (m1 + m2).
reasoning_ladder.represent: Table of states: Case 1 (m1 = F/8), Case 2 (m2 = F/24), Combined (M = m1 + m2).
reasoning_ladder.connect: Newton II: a_combined = F / (m1 + m2) = 1 / (m1/F + m2/F) = 1 / (1/a1 + 1/a2).
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Combined mass accelerates at 6.0 m/s^2 (strictly less than either mass alone).

model_proof.final_expression: a_combined = 6.0 m/s^2.
model_proof.final_answer_value: a_combined = 6.0 m/s^2.

independent_check.quick_check: Adding mass must lower the acceleration below min(a1, a2) = 8 m/s^2; 6 m/s^2 satisfies this.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not average accelerations; mass adds linearly, so accelerations add harmonically.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: From the definition of linear momentum $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$, what do the slopes of a momentum-velocity ($p-v$) graph at fixed mass and a momentum-mass ($p-m$) graph at fixed velocity represent? Furthermore, how is net force related to the momentum curve?

options.A: The slope of p-v equals mass m; the slope of p-m equals velocity v; and the time slope (dp/dt) of a momentum-time graph equals the net force $F_{\text{net}}$.
options.B: The slope of p-v equals velocity; the slope of p-m equals mass; and net force is the area under the momentum-time curve.
options.C: The slope of p-v equals acceleration; the slope of p-m equals impulse; and net force is constant regardless of dp/dt.
options.D: Both graph slopes equal kinetic energy; net force is given by p^2/(2m).

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-06 to SYNTHESIZE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: dp/dv = m (linear slope is mass); dp/dm = v (linear slope is velocity); and Newton II states $F_{\text{net}}$ = dp/dt.

B.diagnostic: Swapped the axes and confused slope with area.

C.diagnostic: Confused velocity with acceleration and momentum with impulse.

D.diagnostic: Confused momentum graphs with kinetic energy formulas.

progressive_hints.prompt_question: Differentiate $p = mv$ with respect to v when mass m is constant.
progressive_hints.reveal_text: dp/dv = m (the slope is mass).

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Differentiate $p = mv$ with respect to m when velocity v is constant.
progressive_hints.reveal_text: dp/dm = v (the slope is velocity).

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does Newton's Second Law say about the time derivative of momentum dp/dt?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $F_{\text{net}}$ = dp/dt (net force equals the rate of change of momentum).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Analyze physical meaning of gradients of p-v, p-m, and p-t graphs.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Graph axes: p vs v (slope = dp/dv); p vs m (slope = dp/dm); p vs t (slope = dp/dt).
reasoning_ladder.connect: From $p = mv$: partial p / partial v = m; partial p / partial m = v; Newton II: $F_{\text{net}}$ = dp/dt.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Gradients represent mass, velocity, and instantaneous net force respectively.

model_proof.final_expression: The slope of p-v equals mass m; the slope of p-m equals velocity v; and the time slope (dp/dt) of a momentum-time graph equals the net force $F_{\text{net}}$.
model_proof.final_answer_value: The slope of p-v equals mass m; the slope of p-m equals velocity v; and the time slope (dp/dt) of a momentum-time graph equals the net force $F_{\text{net}}$.

independent_check.quick_check: Units check: [dp/dv] = (kg m/s)/(m/s) = kg [M]; [dp/dm] = (kg m/s)/kg = m/s [L T^-1]; [dp/dt] = (kg m/s)/s = N [M L T^-2].
independent_check.check_it_another_way: When net force is zero, p-t graph is horizontal (slope = 0), confirming momentum conservation.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not confuse rate of change with area under a curve.

questions.stem: In an ideal Atwood machine with a massless, frictionless pulley, two masses $m_1 = 3.0\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 2.0\text{ kg}$ are connected by a light, inextensible string. Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, determine the system acceleration $a$ and the tension $T$ in the string.

options.A: a = 1.96 m/s^2; T = 23.52 N (the harmonic mean of gravitational weights).

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-04 to SYNTHESIZE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

B.diagnostic: Arithmetic error in denominator sum or tension calculation.

C.diagnostic: Used (m1 - m2)g / m1 for acceleration.

D.diagnostic: Free-fall limit applicable only if m2 = 0.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Treat the Atwood machine as an unrolled 1D system. What is the net driving force?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Net driving force = (m1 - m2)g = (3.0 - 2.0)(9.8) = 9.8 N.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the total system inertia being accelerated by that driving force?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Total inertia = m1 + m2 = 3.0 + 2.0 = 5.0 kg.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How do you evaluate acceleration a and string tension T?

reasoning_ladder.understand: Two masses m1 = 3 kg and m2 = 2 kg are coupled by a light string over a frictionless pulley.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Draw individual FBDs: m1 has downward m1 g and upward T; m2 has downward m2 g and upward T.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Equations of motion: m1 g - T = m1 a; T - m2 g = m2 a.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Acceleration is 1.96 m/s^2; tension is 23.52 N (less than m1 g = 29.4 N, greater than m2 g = 19.6 N).

model_proof.final_expression: a = 1.96 m/s^2; T = 23.52 N (the harmonic mean of gravitational weights).
model_proof.final_answer_value: a = 1.96 m/s^2; T = 23.52 N (the harmonic mean of gravitational weights).

independent_check.quick_check: Tension 23.52 N is strictly between m2 g (19.6 N) and m1 g (29.4 N), as required for acceleration.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Tension formula T = [2 m1 m2 / (m1 + m2)] g represents the harmonic mean of the two gravitational weights.
independent_check.watch_out: Tension is NOT equal to (m1 + m2)g or (m1 - m2)g.

limiting_cases.expected: a = 0, T = m1 g (neutral static equilibrium)
a -> g, T -> 0 (free fall of m1)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A block of mass $m$ rests on a rough ramp whose inclination angle $\theta$ can be varied. The coefficient of static friction is $\mu_s$. Using the Contact Reaction Cone invariant, at what maximum angle $\theta_{\text{repose}}$ can the ramp be tilted before the block slips down?

options.A: tan(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$ (independent of block mass m).
options.B: sin(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$ m g.
options.C: cos(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$ / m.
options.D: theta_repose = 45 deg for all surface materials.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-03 to JUSTIFY demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Reaction vector R = N + f_s must be vertical to balance mg. Max cone angle $\lambda$ satisfies tan($\lambda$) = f_max / N = $\mu_s$. Thus theta_repose = $\lambda$ => tan($\theta$) = $\mu_s$.

B.diagnostic: Dimensional mismatch: sin($\theta$) is dimensionless while $\mu_s$ m g has dimensions of force [M L T^-2].

C.diagnostic: Inverted trigonometric relation and included non-cancelling mass.

D.diagnostic: Angle of repose depends directly on the interface friction coefficient $\mu_s$.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Combine the normal reaction N and friction force f into a single total contact vector R.
progressive_hints.reveal_text: R = N + f. For equilibrium, R must be vertical and collinear with gravity mg.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the maximum angle $\lambda$ between contact reaction vector R and the surface normal?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: tan($\lambda$) = f_max / N = ($\mu_s$ N) / N = $\mu_s$.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Since R is vertical, what is the geometric relationship between the incline angle $\theta$ and cone angle $\lambda$?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: $\theta$ = $\lambda$, meaning slip occurs when tan($\theta$) > $\mu_s$.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Find threshold angle $\theta$ before slip occurs on inclined plane with static friction $\mu_s$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Draw FBD with contact reaction cone: R = N + f, gravity mg downward.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Static equilibrium: R balances mg => R is vertical. Angle between R and normal is $\theta$.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: At slip threshold: f_s = f_max = $\mu_s$ N => tan($\theta$) = f_max / N = $\mu_s$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Repose angle satisfies tan(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$, completely independent of mass m.

model_proof.final_expression: tan(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$ (independent of block mass m).
model_proof.final_answer_value: tan(theta_repose) = $\mu_s$ (independent of block mass m).

independent_check.quick_check: Mass m cancels identically in mg sin($\theta$) = $\mu_s$ mg cos($\theta$).
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Project forces along incline: mg sin($\theta$) <= $\mu_s$ mg cos($\theta$) => tan($\theta$) <= $\mu_s$.
independent_check.watch_out: Angle of repose depends only on surface roughness $\mu_s$, not on block weight.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: Block $A$ of mass $m_1 = 2.0\text{ kg}$ rests on top of block $B$ of mass $m_2 = 3.0\text{ kg}$, which sits on a frictionless horizontal table. The coefficient of static friction between block $A$ and block $B$ is $\mu_s = 0.40$. A horizontal force $F$ is applied to bottom block $B$. What is the maximum force $F_{\max}$ that can be applied without block $A$ slipping relative to block $B$? (Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$).

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-04 to SYNTHESIZE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Top block A has max acceleration a_max = ($\mu_s$ m1 g)/m1 = $\mu_s$ g = 3.92 m/s^2. For no slip, both blocks accelerate together: F_max = (m1 + m2) a_max = (m1 + m2) $\mu_s$ g = 19.6 N.

B.diagnostic: Considers only the friction force on A rather than the total force accelerating both masses.

C.diagnostic: Uses bottom block mass instead of normal force between A and B.

D.diagnostic: Divided total force by 2 without physical justification.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the only horizontal force that can accelerate top block A forward?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Static friction f_s from the top surface of block B.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What is the maximum horizontal acceleration that friction can impart to block A?

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: If both blocks move together at a_max, what total horizontal force F_max must pull the composite mass (m1 + m2)?

reasoning_ladder.understand: m1 = 2 kg on m2 = 3 kg on smooth table; static friction $\mu_s$ = 0.40 between blocks. Find max F on m2 for no slip.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Draw FBD for m1: forward friction f_s. For m2: forward pull F, backward friction f_s from m1.
reasoning_ladder.connect: No slip condition: a1 = a2 = a <= a_max. Max friction on m1: f_max = $\mu_s$ m1 g.
reasoning_ladder.calculate: a_max = f_max / m1 = $\mu_s$ g = 3.92 m/s^2. System force: F_max = (m1 + m2) a_max = 5.0 * 3.92 = 19.6 N.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Maximum pull force without slip is exactly 19.6 N.

independent_check.check_it_another_way: In accelerated frame of B, pseudo force on A is m1 a; slip occurs when m1 a > $\mu_s$ m1 g => a > $\mu_s$ g.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not use $\mu_s$ (m1 + m2)g as friction; normal force at interface is m1 g, not (m1 + m2)g.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: An ideal movable pulley supports a load of mass $M = 20\text{ kg}$ ($W = M g = 196\text{ N}$). A person pulls the free end of the light string upward with an effort force $F$. Assuming frictionless, massless pulleys and an inextensible string, what effort force $F$ is required to hold the load in static equilibrium, and what is the mechanical advantage?

options.A: Effort force F = W/2 = 98 N; Mechanical Advantage = 2.
options.B: Effort force F = W = 196 N; Mechanical Advantage = 1.
options.C: Effort force F = 2W = 392 N; Mechanical Advantage = 0.5.
options.D: Effort force F = W/4 = 49 N; Mechanical Advantage = 4.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-04 to SYNTHESIZE demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: String length L = 2 y_pulley + y_free => Delta x_input = 2 Delta y_load. By virtual work: F * (2 $\Delta y$) = W * $\Delta y$ => F = W/2 = 98 N. MA = W/F = 2.

B.diagnostic: Applies to a fixed pulley, which changes direction but provides no mechanical advantage.

C.diagnostic: Inverted the mechanical advantage, assuming lifting effort must be doubled.

D.diagnostic: Assumes a 4-pulley compound block-and-tackle rather than a single movable pulley.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: How many string segments directly support the movable pulley and its load W?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Two vertical string segments, each carrying string tension T.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What does vertical force balance on the massless movable pulley require?

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Since the person pulls the continuous string, effort force F equals tension T. What is F and MA?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: F = T = W / 2 = 196 / 2 = 98 N. Mechanical Advantage MA = W / F = 2.

reasoning_ladder.understand: Load W = 196 N supported by an ideal movable pulley; find effort force F and MA.
reasoning_ladder.represent: FBD of movable pulley: upward 2T, downward load W. Inextensible string constraint.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Kinematic constraint: Delta x_effort = 2 Delta y_load. Virtual work: W_in = W_out => F(2 $\Delta y$) = W $\Delta y$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Effort force is halved (98 N) with a mechanical advantage of 2.

model_proof.final_expression: Effort force F = W/2 = 98 N; Mechanical Advantage = 2.
model_proof.final_answer_value: Effort force F = W/2 = 98 N; Mechanical Advantage = 2.

independent_check.quick_check: Work conservation: pulling 2 meters with 98 N gives 196 J; lifting 196 N by 1 meter requires 196 J.
independent_check.check_it_another_way: Newton II on massless pulley: $\Sigma F_y = 2T - W = 0 \implies T = W/2$.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not forget that effort displacement is twice load displacement.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.stem: A conical pendulum consists of a small bob of mass $m = 0.50\text{ kg}$ suspended by a light string of length $L = 1.0\text{ m}$ revolving at constant speed in a horizontal circle of radius $r$, with the string making a constant angle $\theta = 60^\circ$ to the vertical. Taking $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, what are the string tension $T$ and the net horizontal centripetal force $F_{\text{net}}$?

options.A: Tension T = mg / cos(60 deg) = 9.80 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = mg tan(60 deg) = 4.90 sqrt(3) N approx 8.49 N.
options.B: Tension T = mg cos(60 deg) = 2.45 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = mg sin(60 deg) = 4.24 N.
options.C: Tension T = mg = 4.90 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = 0 N because speed is constant.
options.D: Tension T = 2mg sin(60 deg) = 8.49 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = 9.80 N.

qrt_contract.protected_work_W: Rigorous physical reasoning execution connecting NLM-03 to JUSTIFY demand.

rival_demands.rejection_rationale: Requires dynamic physical reasoning, not isolated recall.

A.diagnostic: Correct: Vertical equilibrium: T cos($\theta$) = mg => T = mg/cos(60 deg) = 0.50(9.8)/0.5 = 9.80 N. Horizontal net force: $F_{\text{net}}$ = T sin($\theta$) = mg tan(60 deg) = 4.90 * sqrt(3) = 8.49 N.

B.diagnostic: Inverted trigonometric component: multiplied by cos($\theta$) instead of dividing.

C.diagnostic: Assumes constant speed implies zero net force, ignoring circular centripetal acceleration.

D.diagnostic: Formula misapplication in resolving orthogonal components.

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 1: What is the Key Physics?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What forces act on the bob, and along which axes do they resolve?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: Tension T along the string and gravity mg downward. Resolve T into horizontal T sin($\theta$) and vertical T cos($\theta$).

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 2: How Would You Represent It?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: Is there any vertical acceleration for the bob revolving in a horizontal circle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: No; $a_y$ = 0, so T cos($\theta$) = mg => T = mg / cos($\theta$).

progressive_hints.title: Hint Tier 3: What Would You Write First?
progressive_hints.prompt_question: What provides the net centripetal force directed toward the center of the horizontal circle?
progressive_hints.reveal_text: The horizontal component of tension: $F_{\text{net}}$ = T sin($\theta$) = mg tan($\theta$).

reasoning_ladder.understand: Bob of mass m = 0.50 kg revolves at angle $\theta$ = 60 deg to vertical; find T and horizontal $F_{\text{net}}$.
reasoning_ladder.represent: Draw FBD of bob: downward mg, tension T at angle $\theta$ to vertical.
reasoning_ladder.connect: Vertical equilibrium: $\Sigma F_y = T \cos\theta - mg = 0$. Horizontal dynamics: $\Sigma F_x = T \sin\theta = F_{\text{net}}$.
reasoning_ladder.interpret: Tension is 9.80 N; net horizontal centripetal force is 8.49 N.

model_proof.final_expression: Tension T = mg / cos(60 deg) = 9.80 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = mg tan(60 deg) = 4.90 sqrt(3) N approx 8.49 N.
model_proof.final_answer_value: Tension T = mg / cos(60 deg) = 9.80 N; Net horizontal force $F_{\text{net}}$ = mg tan(60 deg) = 4.90 sqrt(3) N approx 8.49 N.

independent_check.quick_check: T = 9.80 N is greater than mg = 4.90 N, which is required because T must support weight and provide horizontal acceleration.
independent_check.watch_out: Do not assume net force is zero merely because speed is constant in uniform circular motion.
